issues.legal_issue: A second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be admitted on factual questions or used to unsettle concurrent findings of fact without a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concurrently found that the claimants had not proved title by adverse possession and that a landlord-tenant relationship existed.
The High Court framed questions that concerned the identity of the land, the evidence, and the validity of a gift deed, then reconsidered the matters at length and set aside the concurrent judgments.

The Supreme Court found that the framed questions were essentially factual, were not debatable substantial questions of law, and that the findings below were not shown to be perverse or contrary to law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no proper basis to admit the second appeals on the framed questions or interfere with the concurrent factual findings; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC requires a substantial question of law involved in the case, which must be formulated before a second appeal is heard. A question must be real and debatable, materially affect the parties’ rights, arise from the pleadings and sustainable factual findings, and be necessary to decide the case. The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence merely because another factual view is possible, absent a perverse finding or an error of law. The Court relied on Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari (2001) 3 SCC 179, including its discussion of Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. Century Spg. and Mfg. Co. Ltd. (AIR 1962 SC 1314), and Thiagarajan v. Sri Venugopalaswamy B. Koil (2004) 5 SCC 762; it also referred to Kshitish Chandra Purkait, Panchugopal Barua, and Kondiba Dagadu Kadam.

rule.if: second_appeal and (questions_are_only_factual or no_debatable_substantial_law_question) and concurrent_findings_are_evidence_based and not findings_are_perverse_or_legally_erroneous

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.questions_are_only_factual: The questions presented concern factual matters or reappreciation of evidence rather than a substantial legal issue.
predicates.no_debatable_substantial_law_question: No debatable question of law materially affecting the parties’ rights arises from the pleadings and findings.
predicates.concurrent_findings_are_evidence_based: The lower courts reached the same factual findings on the evidence before them.
predicates.findings_are_perverse_or_legally_erroneo: The concurrent findings are so unsupported or contrary to law that they cannot stand.

issues.definition: When a second appeal presents only factual questions and rests on evidence-based concurrent findings that are not perverse or legally erroneous, the findings cannot be reopened without a substantial question of law.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot remand a case for a new trial without a properly raised and supported basis for remand and a reasoned decision under the applicable remand provisions.
material_facts: No party sought remand before the first appellate court or the High Court, and no complaint was made that the trial had been unsatisfactory or had caused prejudice.
The High Court framed no substantial question of law concerning remand, identified no applicable remand ground, and ordered a de novo trial in all the suits.
The High Court set aside the lower courts’ decisions and remanded the cases of its own initiative.
issues.conclusion: The remand order was unjustified and beyond the High Court’s jurisdiction in the circumstances; the High Court should have decided the appeals on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rules 23, 23-A and 25 CPC govern remand by an appellate court. A party seeking remand must raise the plea and establish a factual basis bringing the case within an applicable rule; the appellate court must record reasons for the remand. Section 100 CPC confines a second appeal to formulated questions, so the High Court could not decide an unframed remand issue.

rule.if: appellate_case and remand_not_sought_by_a_party and no_supported_remand_ground and no_remand_question_framed

predicates.appellate_case: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court is considering whether to send the case back for further proceedings.
predicates.remand_not_sought_by_a_party: No party raised a request for remand before the appellate court.
predicates.no_supported_remand_ground: No facts were established showing an applicable basis for remand or prejudice requiring further trial proceedings.
predicates.no_remand_question_framed: The appellate court did not frame a question authorizing it to decide whether remand was warranted.

issues.definition: If no party seeks remand, no factual basis for it is established, and the issue is not framed for decision, the appellate court cannot order remand on its own.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who asserts title solely through adverse possession must prove that claim with satisfactory evidence.
material_facts: The claimants asserted title against the State through alleged continuous possession by their predecessors and themselves for about a century.
They did not rely on a grant, lease deed, or patta from the State.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the evidence was inadequate to establish adverse possession, and no error of law in that finding was shown.
issues.conclusion: The claimants failed to prove title by adverse possession, and the concurrent finding against their claim stood.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of proving a pleaded claim of adverse possession lies on the claimant, who must support it with satisfactory evidence. A finding on that factual question, when concurrently made and not shown to contain an error of law, is binding in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC.

rule.if: civil_title_claim and title_claimed_only_by_adverse_possession and claimant_bears_burden and evidence_is_insufficient and concurrent_finding_against_claim

predicates.civil_title_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to title to property.
predicates.title_claimed_only_by_adverse_possession: The claimant relies solely on possession said to have been adverse to the asserted owner.
predicates.claimant_bears_burden: The party asserting adverse possession is responsible for proving it.
predicates.evidence_is_insufficient: The evidence does not satisfactorily establish the asserted adverse possession.
predicates.concurrent_finding_against_claim: The lower courts have both found that the claimant failed to prove adverse possession.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies solely on adverse possession for title and the evidence is insufficient, a concurrent finding against the claim means that title by adverse possession is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent factual finding establishing a landlord-tenant relationship cannot be displaced in a second appeal without a basis for disturbing that finding under the governing limits on second appeals.
material_facts: The landowner alleged that the occupant had been inducted as a tenant under a lease and sought eviction.
The trial court found that the landlord-tenant relationship was established, and the first appellate court affirmed that finding.
The Supreme Court found no error in the first appellate court’s judgment.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the landlord-tenant relationship existed was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 CPC, a second appellate court cannot substitute its factual findings for concurrent findings based on evidence merely because another view may be possible. The Court relied on Thiagarajan v. Sri Venugopalaswamy B. Koil (2004) 5 SCC 762 and the principles stated in Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari (2001) 3 SCC 179.

rule.if: second_appeal and landlord_tenant_relationship_found_by_lower_courts and concurrent_finding_is_evidence_based and not finding_is_perverse_or_legally_erroneous

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_found_by_lo: The lower courts found that a landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties.
predicates.concurrent_finding_is_evidence_based: Both lower courts reached that finding on the evidence before them.
predicates.finding_is_perverse_or_legally_erroneous: The finding is so unsupported or contrary to law that it cannot stand.

issues.definition: An evidence-based concurrent finding of a landlord-tenant relationship stands in a second appeal unless it is perverse or legally erroneous.

issues.legal_issue: A gift between members of a claimant’s family is not material to a dispute in which title is claimed solely by adverse possession against another asserted owner.
material_facts: The claimants’ pleaded basis for title was adverse possession against the State, not a grant or transfer from the State.
A question concerning a gift between two members of the claimants’ family was framed in the second appeal.
The Supreme Court found that the gift’s execution or validity did not assist in deciding the claim of title by adverse possession against the State.
issues.conclusion: The gift question was irrelevant to the principal title dispute and did not constitute a substantial question of law arising from the case.
issues.legal_principle: A question must arise from the case and be necessary to decide it to qualify as a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC. A transaction between members of the claimant’s family does not resolve a title claim founded solely on adverse possession against a different asserted owner.

predicates.title_dispute_based_only_on_adverse_poss: The claimant bases the title dispute solely on alleged adverse possession against the person or entity asserting ownership.
predicates.gift_is_between_claimant_family_members: The disputed gift is a transaction between members of the claimant’s family.
predicates.gift_does_not_affect_the_adverse_possess: The gift has no bearing on whether the claimant acquired title by adverse possession against the asserted owner.

issues.definition: A family gift that does not affect a title claim based solely on adverse possession is irrelevant to that title dispute.
